segments.title: Repairing capability before buying new equipment
segments.body: Procurement is a force-structure problem rather than a shopping list. New money should first reinforce programs already under way and restore capabilities previously cut to the bone. Buying more of an existing aircraft may be cheaper than adding a second type with a superficially attractive unit price. A new type duplicates logistics, training, basing, command, certification, safety, consultation, and business-case costs, while an enlarged existing fleet can use support arrangements already in place. The relevant price is the complete supported capability, not just the advertised platform.

evidence.note: The opening contrasts reinforcing existing programs and cut capabilities with the urge to buy new equipment.
The aircraft example explains why extra types bring duplicated logistics, training, basing, safety, and approval costs.

segments.summary: A procurement warning starts with the habit of chasing new equipment before reinforcing existing programs, support lines, and hollowed-out capabilities.

segments.title: Why weapons and warships should not be called toys
segments.body: Calling military equipment toys disguises its human cost. A tank carries a crew whose lives may be lost if the vehicle is destroyed, while even a standard escort can put more than two hundred sailors at risk. Casual language makes procurement sound like an enthusiast's shopping exercise instead of a decision about whether people receive equipment capable of protecting them. The word appears here only to criticize the political appetite for novelty. This ethical objection is why the procurement framework begins with supported capability and human consequences rather than fascination with a new platform.

evidence.note: The transcript rejects describing tanks and warships as toys because their destruction can kill the crews inside them, while explaining why the term is used critically in the procurement discussion.

segments.summary: Calling tanks, warships, and other military equipment toys obscures the lives placed at risk when those systems fail in combat.

segments.title: Industrial politics shaping defence choices
segments.body: British and French industrial politics lead into US Navy surface-combatant decisions. The CV90 should at least have been considered for Ajax despite the Ministry of Defence's dispute with BAE, and a French yard dispute should not have shaped construction of a capital ship expected to serve for decades. In the United States, the failure of Zumwalt's intended railgun did not erase the value of the ship's newer power and engineering architecture. A limited production run might have bridged the fleet toward a true Arleigh Burke replacement while the Navy retired Ticonderoga-class cruisers and struggled with the Littoral Combat Ship program. Political hostility or one failed subsystem should not erase the wider capability a program can still provide.

evidence.note: BAE/CV90 exclusion in Ajax and French yard politics around carrier construction.
The US examples compare Zumwalt cancellation, Arleigh Burke modernization pressure, and LCS persistence.

segments.summary: Examples from Ajax, French carrier construction, Zumwalt, Arleigh Burke, and LCS show how politics and program momentum can distort procurement choices.

segments.title: Accepting mistakes before copying another navy
segments.body: No nation, institution, or political culture is immune to mistakes. Procurement remains a human activity, so ego, rivalry, and short-term politics will intrude regardless of the system making the decision. Demanding equipment that resembles another country's successful platform can also substitute familiarity for analysis. A domestic design may better meet national requirements even when it does not copy the admired foreign example. Sound procurement begins by acknowledging fallibility and judging equipment against the buyer's own circumstances.

evidence.note: The argument that every country remains human and therefore capable of procurement mistakes regardless of political system or culture.
Politics and the desire to copy equipment already operated by another country identified as further distortions.

segments.summary: No political system or national culture eliminates procurement error, and copying an ally's equipment can substitute appearance for a force designed around domestic needs.

segments.title: Know the nation before buying the force
segments.body: The country itself comes before any list of external threats. Trade exposure and transport routes determine whether maritime, rail, or air links require protection. Demography and employment conditions shape whether the armed forces can rely on abundant personnel or must favor systems that use scarce people efficiently. A government may import complete equipment, assemble foreign components, or retain domestic research and production. The British tanker example shows that even building hulls abroad and finishing them at home can become politically consequential when voters and shipyards expect defence spending to sustain local work. Procurement therefore begins with an honest account of national economics, labor, industry, and political expectations.

evidence.note: The transcript asks what kind of country is buying the force, including trade routes, demography, and employment context.
The discussion turns to industrial base, imports, domestic finishing, tanker hulls, British yards, BAE, and political views of procurement.

segments.summary: The procurement framework starts with national self-knowledge: trade exposure, demography, economy, industrial base, imports, domestic yards, and political expectations.

segments.title: Choosing what a national defence industry must preserve
segments.body: A national defence industry can mean different things in different countries. British politics often prioritizes the physical location of work even when the yard's corporate owner is foreign, while France generally places more weight on both French construction and French ownership. The United States also accepts foreign-owned suppliers such as BAE when production and employment remain inside America. In Britain, keeping Appledore and Harland & Wolff active shows how support for yards can become a political consequence of earlier decisions to build support-ship hulls abroad. Domestic construction can narrow competition because a specialized yard may become the only plausible bidder for a class of ship. The Type 31 yard and discussion of a future Type 32 show why governments must decide how procurement should balance security, employment, and industrial resilience.

evidence.note: Imported tanker hulls, pressure to sustain British yards, Appledore and Harland & Wolff, and the political preference for work performed in Britain.
Comparison of French, American, and British rules about ownership and location; how limited domestic facilities can create single-source shipbuilding choices.
The passage asks whether procurement is being judged principally through national employment or security.

segments.summary: British, French, and American approaches to ownership, domestic construction, employment, and yard capacity show that industrial policy is part of the requirement rather than a cost-free procurement preference.

segments.title: Matching ships to threats and roles
segments.body: The early United States Navy's heavy frigates separate successful role design from complete force design. Those ships made sense against Barbary corsairs and could win valuable single-ship actions and conduct commerce raiding. They could not replace ships of the line when the opponent was the Royal Navy's full battle fleet. Congress authorized heavier ships but failed to ensure that they were built before the War of 1812. The strategic effect reached beyond prestige: American raiders could not challenge British concentration around the South American silver trade that supported commerce with China and British operations in India. A platform can excel in its intended role while leaving a decisive threat unanswered.

evidence.note: Comparison of heavy frigates against Barbary threats with the need for ships of the line against the Royal Navy.
The War of 1812 passage links absent ships of the line, raiding choices, protected South American silver traffic, and wider strategic limits.

segments.summary: The War of 1812 example shows why heavy frigates solve some threats but cannot replace ships of the line when the opponent and mission set change.

segments.title: Geography turns procurement into strategy
segments.body: Geography determines the route by which danger can reach the homeland and therefore which services procurement must favor. A long land frontier can absorb army funding and personnel, while a mountain-locked state may emphasize air defence, fortified passes, and reserves sufficient to survive isolation. A maritime or island state must ask how global trade, alliances, airborne attack, and seaborne assault shape its force. Defending the home may mean keeping an opponent beyond the sea approaches rather than waiting to fight at the coast. The same logic applies to the continental United States, whose scale does not remove the Atlantic and Pacific from its defensive depth. Distant threats can look irrelevant to a public protected by those oceans even when trade, communications, and forward defence depend on controlling them.

evidence.note: Land borders create an army burden, while a mountain-locked state needs air defence, fortified passes, and stockpiles.
The transcript asks whether the country is maritime or island-based, dependent on global trade, alliance-bound, or facing airborne, seaborne, or land threats.
The passage develops defensive depth, overseas conflict distance, and the political case for maritime procurement.

segments.summary: A country's maritime exposure, alliances, defensive depth, and expeditionary obligations shape what it must buy and what it can afford to ignore.

segments.title: Including political resilience in threat assessment
segments.body: Threat assessment extends beyond a list of foreign armed forces. A large state may possess resources at home yet remain unable or unwilling to exploit them because environmental protections and other political choices are part of what the society seeks to preserve. Mature political systems can become vulnerable when conventions are treated as self-enforcing and citizens no longer understand why institutions work as they do. Short political messaging is older than social media: headlines, slogans, and gossip have always shaped public life. Kaiser Wilhelm's public preferences for British officeholders show how even a simple expression of support can complicate another government's appointments. Modern planners must distinguish states, non-state organizations, and competing institutions within a country, since some may be friendly while a foreign or defence ministry is hostile. Procurement cannot follow sensibly until the state understands both the external danger and the political system it is trying to defend.

evidence.note: Domestic resources, environmental protection, political conventions, and civic renewal all shape national resilience.
Headlines, short political messages, gossip, and attempts to influence politics are presented as longstanding human practices rather than inventions of social media.
Kaiser Wilhelm's public preferences for British officeholders illustrate a simple form of foreign political interference.
Internal and external threats, state and non-state organizations, and hostile institutions within an otherwise mixed foreign state distinguished.

segments.summary: Resource choices, environmental protections, political conventions, foreign influence, and divisions inside other states all affect the threats a defence plan must address.

segments.title: Buying forces to manage conflict before war
segments.body: Military procurement helps manage conflict before and during war, as well as supplying forces for combat. Conflict management here covers deterrence, minimization, and pacification or termination. Deterrence may rely on conspicuous force or diplomatic signaling, while minimization can isolate an opponent by building relationships that deny it allies and prevent a wider war. If those measures fail, the force still needs the means to stop the conflict on acceptable terms. A minimal inventory may be insufficient because preventing escalation can require an overwhelming capability the country can credibly deploy. Depending on geography and national strengths, that might be a carrier battle group, a strike-bomber force, an armored division, or a combination of them.

evidence.note: The transcript divides conflict management into deterrence, minimization through diplomatic isolation, and pacification or conflict termination.
Deterrence's possible requirement for deployable overwhelming force, with carrier, bomber, and armored formations as national alternatives.

segments.summary: Procurement supports deterrence, diplomatic isolation, and conflict termination as well as combat, so the right form of overwhelming force depends on what a country can deploy credibly.

segments.title: Designing a coherent British flight-deck force
segments.body: The Queen Elizabeth-class carriers should have sat inside a larger flight-deck plan rather than being judged as an isolated purchase. Replacing Ocean, Albion, Bulwark, and the landing ships with purpose-designed amphibious ships could have produced two strike-oriented decks alongside three amphibious decks and large docks. The American class is not a direct template because its internal organization is built around United States amphibious practice. British ships would need their own aviation, troop, landing-craft, and command balance designed in from the outset. The same systems-level shortfall appears in the small Type 45 destroyer buy. Omitting Mark 41 vertical-launch cells at construction also denied those ships an easier route to weapons such as SM-3 and Tomahawk. A coherent force package can be lost when each platform program is decided separately.

evidence.note: The transcript proposes pairing two strike carriers with three amphibious flight decks and docks designed around British expeditionary requirements.
The short Type 45 buy and absence of Mark 41 cells for SM-3 and Tomahawk identified as related procurement choices.

segments.summary: A British force-design example links the Queen Elizabeth class to amphibious flight decks, docks, escorts, and missile capacity instead of evaluating each ship program alone.

segments.title: Procurement risk after the Cold War
segments.body: Post-Cold War procurement rested for years on two unusually optimistic assumptions. The first held that peer conflict was remote and that major powers would fight only wars they chose to enter. The second claimed that governments had mastered the economic cycle and could plan around steadily improving finances. Kosovo, the Gulf conflicts, 9/11, and numerous smaller wars did not immediately dislodge this outlook. The economy resembles the sea in one respect: it can support those who respect its limits, but it cannot be commanded into permanent calm. A resilient force plan must survive security and fiscal shocks instead of depending on reassuring political forecasts.

evidence.note: Post-1991 procurement assumed remote peer conflict, wars of choice, and permanent economic improvement.
The passage compares economic confidence to treating the sea as controllable and concludes that governments did not have the world securely in hand.

segments.summary: The lecture criticizes post-Cold War assumptions that peer conflict was remote, wars would be optional, and economic growth could carry defence plans indefinitely.

segments.title: Putting logistics first in the capability hierarchy
segments.body: The requirement hierarchy separates essentials, necessaries, and desirable capabilities. Logistics should not sit in a separate adjustable category beneath the visible combat systems. Logistics and infrastructure are essentials because every ship, aircraft, weapon, and formation depends on them before it can generate useful force. The size of the support network may expand with the force, but its existence is not optional. Nuclear weapons show how national position changes the rest of the hierarchy: among nuclear peers they may form an essential deterrent ceiling and discourage chemical or biological escalation. They do not prevent every conventional clash, so the framework still has to fund usable conventional forces below that ceiling.

evidence.note: The transcript defines three capability tiers and argues that logistics and infrastructure belong in the essential tier.
The nuclear-weapons example shows how peer status and escalation risks shape a nation's essential capabilities.

segments.summary: A three-tier framework separates essential, necessary, and desirable capabilities while placing logistics and infrastructure firmly among the essentials.

segments.title: Warships, weapons, and the moral weight of command
segments.body: Affection for warships is distinct from approval of the violence for which weapons are built. Ships embody engineering and history, and the people required to fight them deserve respect, but no weapon is inherently pleasant or harmless. Combat places service personnel in extreme conditions and can force them to choose between dangers to themselves and terrible consequences for others. That burden makes confident claims about easy wartime decisions deeply misleading. Wellington's observation that only a lost battle is worse than a won one emphasizes that even victory carries suffering. Procurement therefore has an ethical dimension because equipment choices shape the circumstances in which real people must act.

evidence.note: The transcript rejects glorification, distinguishes affection for warships from liking weapons, and describes the severe decisions military personnel may face.
Wellington's comparison of a battle won with a battle lost invoked to emphasize command's moral burden.

segments.summary: Admiration for warships and respect for their crews are separated from glorifying weapons or treating combat decisions as easy.

segments.title: Credible deterrence requires willingness to act
segments.body: Political intent determines whether technical capability has deterrent value. A carrier battle group can possess aircraft and long-range missiles able to strike enemy bases and infrastructure, yet those systems matter only if leaders can imagine authorizing their use. If national policy rules out such action under every plausible condition, buying the weapons wastes resources that could support capabilities the country will employ. The same contradiction undermines deterrence before combat begins. An opponent must believe both that the weapon works and that the government is prepared to order it into action. Force design therefore has to connect equipment, doctrine, and political willingness rather than treating the platform as a deterrent by itself.

evidence.note: The question of political authorization for carrier strikes against enemy bases, with unused strike capabilities judged wasted procurement.
Deterrence depends on an opponent believing that the capability will actually be used.

segments.summary: Strike aircraft and long-range missiles have little deterrent value when national leaders and adversaries both know the country will not authorize their use.

segments.title: Designing expeditionary forces for the theatre
segments.body: Three expeditionary problems show why the label alone cannot define a force. A European commitment may need an armored or mechanized division with enough tanks, cavalry, infantry carriers, and mobility to participate in maneuver warfare. NATO's northern flank instead calls for a self-sufficient infantry-heavy brigade suited to mountainous Arctic terrain and able to move along the coast or insert under fire. Britain might send a continental formation through the Channel Tunnel or across the narrow seas in commercial roll-on/roll-off shipping if the rear area is secure. The United States faces a longer transatlantic problem and may prefer to pre-position equipment and fly personnel forward. Moving complete formations by sea creates convoys and consumes escorts, linking army readiness directly to sealift and naval force structure.

evidence.note: A European commitment may require an armoured formation for continental manoeuvre, while NATO's Arctic flank calls for a self-sufficient brigade capable of coastal movement and protected insertion.
Comparison of British movement into Europe with American pre-positioning, sealift, Atlantic convoys, and the resulting escort demand.

segments.summary: European maneuver warfare, the Arctic northern flank, and transatlantic reinforcement demand different formations, transport plans, and naval protection.

segments.title: Why open procurement systems expose their failures
segments.body: Western procurement supplies many familiar bad examples partly because its failures are visible. In Britain, the United States, Canada, France, Italy, and Denmark, much of the decision-making is public enough to generate records, reporting, and argument. Defence may not dominate mass politics, but a specialist community still sustains regular scrutiny. Visible criticism does not by itself prove that open systems make more mistakes than opaque ones. It may show that failures, tradeoffs, and contested choices are easier to observe. Procurement records should therefore be compared with each country's level of transparency in mind.

evidence.note: Public decision-making in several Western countries makes their procurement problems easier to identify.
Continuing specialist military discussion despite limited general attention to defence.

segments.summary: British, American, Canadian, French, Italian, and Danish procurement mistakes are easy to cite partly because their decisions receive public scrutiny and sustained specialist debate.

segments.title: Making budgets match real requirements
segments.body: Requirements eventually become budget choices: spend more, cut costs, accept foreign production, pay the domestic premium, or seek partners. Off-the-shelf prices can mislead when local assembly requires a new factory, transferred specialists, worker training, and a short national production run. The British-Dutch amphibious vessel example shows why joint development helps only when partners first agree on compatible ships. The two navies appeared to differ over tonnage and self-defence, including whether the ships required a surface-to-air missile and substantial gun armament. A common family of hulls might share some systems, but partners can still end up funding separate ends of the design family while buying command and weapon systems elsewhere. Preserving every capability only on paper by hollowing out its people, support, and readiness leaves a force unable to act when a crisis arrives.

evidence.note: Matching requirements to a budget can mean spending more, lowering costs, buying abroad, or accepting the full factory and training costs of local production.
The British-Dutch amphibious program example covers mismatched ship size, self-defence firepower, common platforms, and the limits of partnering.

segments.summary: The budget section weighs raising spending, reducing costs, off-the-shelf buying, domestic production premiums, alliances, and failed common requirements.

segments.title: Counting the full cost of domestic production
segments.body: Budget matching begins with a hard choice between spending more and reducing costs. A country that normally builds its own equipment may obtain more platforms by importing from an established foreign factory, but domestic employment and industrial policy can justify paying a premium. That tradeoff should be stated openly rather than hidden behind the mature factory's export price. Building a new facility adds capital expense, while specialists must move to train the workforce or local personnel must travel to the original plant. Those setup and training costs are spread across the buyer's production run, which can erase an apparently attractive unit-price advantage. Industrial sovereignty must be costed as a capability choice rather than treated as free.

evidence.note: Comparison of raising spending, reducing costs, importing from an established factory, and paying a political premium for domestic construction.
New factories, transferred specialists, and workforce training as additions to national production-run costs.

segments.summary: An off-the-shelf unit price is not the cost of a domestic production program once a country adds factories, specialist transfers, training, and a short national run.

segments.title: Why British and Dutch amphibious requirements diverged
segments.body: A partnership cannot save money until both navies want compatible ships. British thinking appeared to favor vessels above 10,000 tons, while the Dutch requirement was below that threshold. The British concept also leaned toward stronger organic self-defence, potentially including CAMM or Sea Ceptor and gun options associated with the Type 31, such as 57 mm or 40 mm Bofors weapons. Those differences affect displacement, internal volume, sensors, magazines, crew, and cost rather than merely changing a few optional fittings. The partners nevertheless entered development before resolving what each expected the ship to do. Money intended to reduce costs can be wasted when a common program begins before a common operational requirement exists.

evidence.note: The joint amphibious program and British interest in point-defence missiles and gun armament, including CAMM, Sea Ceptor, 57 mm, and 40 mm options.
Dutch interest in a ship below 10,000 tons compared with a British design above 10,000 tons, with criticism of development begun before agreeing on the requirement.

segments.summary: A proposed British-Dutch amphibious program exposed incompatible expectations for ship size and self-defence before the partners had agreed on a common requirement.

segments.title: The limits of a common amphibious ship family
segments.body: A family of ships built from a common platform looks like a way to reconcile different British and Dutch requirements. The idea resembles vehicle manufacturing, where a standard foundation is adapted for several products. One navy may still pay to develop the large end of the family while the other finances the small end, leaving little truly shared design work. Command-and-control and weapon systems may already be bought off the shelf, especially for amphibious ships that do not require the bespoke combat systems of high-end air-warfare destroyers or anti-submarine frigates. Landing craft form another procurement problem rather than an automatic common saving. Any claimed saving depends on identifying which expensive systems the partners genuinely share.

evidence.note: The transcript considers a common family of adaptable hulls but notes that Britain and the Netherlands could end up funding different ends of the range while buying command and weapon systems off the shelf.
The warning that an attractive-sounding common procurement arrangement is not necessarily a good one.

segments.summary: A shared hull family can adapt to different missions, but savings shrink when partners finance opposite ends of the design range and buy major systems separately.

segments.title: Why American amphibious ships do not fit British needs
segments.body: Britain cannot simply buy whatever the United States builds. American amphibious vessels span a wide scale, with the largest landing helicopter docks exceeding 40,000 tons. At that displacement they resemble light fleet carriers and can exceed the size of historical treaty battleships. Such ships embody American operating methods, manpower, and global force structure rather than a neutral amphibious template. They would be too large and crew-intensive for the British requirement under discussion. Successful allied equipment must still be judged against the buyer's own doctrine and resources.

evidence.note: Large American LHDs reach light-carrier scale and are too large and crew-intensive for British needs.

segments.summary: American amphibious designs are too large and personnel-intensive for the British requirement, so an allied design is not automatically a suitable purchase.

segments.title: The danger of preserving capability only on paper
segments.body: Budget matching requires a political choice among paying more, trimming lower priorities, accepting reduced versions of necessary capabilities, or finding partners. Raising taxes and forming alliances are real options when all desired equipment cannot survive unchanged. The dishonest alternative is to hollow every capability while retaining the platform names and organizational labels. A force can then appear complete on paper even though shortages of people, support, stores, training, or readiness prevent it from acting. The failure may remain hidden until a crisis reveals that the nominal capability cannot be used. Procurement must fund complete, sustainable forces rather than protect the appearance of breadth.

evidence.note: Cuts, higher taxes, alliances, and partners can reconcile a budget with force requirements.
Hollowing every capability so that it exists on paper but cannot act when trouble arrives.

segments.summary: When spending, cuts, and partnerships cannot reconcile requirements with resources, hollowing every capability preserves an impressive inventory but leaves no force ready for crisis.

segments.title: Giving procurement programs time to work
segments.body: The Boxer program and modern ministerial turnover show why constant changes can damage long procurement cycles. When ministers or senior officers each try to mark a program as their own, an eighteen-month leadership tenure is badly mismatched with development that may last twenty or thirty years. Buying off the shelf does not abolish that timescale because another organization still has to sustain the research and testing that puts advanced equipment on the shelf. Warhammer 40,000 illustrates the opposite danger: freezing innovation entirely while rivals continue to develop. French practice offers a partial stabilizer by legislating major decisions so that a successor must openly pass new legislation to reverse them. Defence reporting creates another problem when it treats every new system as either revolutionary or worthless. Rigorous trials should expose faults before crews depend on the equipment in a war zone, so visible test failures can show that the development process is doing necessary work.

evidence.note: The Boxer program illustrates how ministerial and officer turnover disrupts procurement cycles too long to redirect every few years.
The final procurement lesson discusses legislating decisions, media extremes about new systems, and the value of finding problems in testing.

segments.summary: The closing procurement lesson warns against constant leadership churn and argues that testing problems are better found before combat.

segments.title: When leadership tenure is shorter than procurement
segments.body: Time is one of the hardest procurement constraints. Britain's repeated entry into and withdrawal from the Boxer program illustrates how policy churn can disrupt a long-running project. Ministers and senior officers are tempted to place their own stamp on a program, claim its success, or distinguish themselves from a predecessor. That behavior was less damaging when a ship might move from design through commissioning within roughly three years and a minister remained in post for a similar period. Modern development can last twenty or thirty years while a minister may serve only eighteen months, making repeated redirection structurally destructive. Buying off the shelf does not remove the long cycle because another institution must still fund and perform the research that creates the equipment available to buy.

evidence.note: The transcript uses Boxer and the desire of ministers and senior officers to mark programs as their own to illustrate procurement instability.
Comparison of older shipbuilding and leadership timescales with modern twenty- or thirty-year development; why off-the-shelf procurement still depends on long research programs.

segments.summary: Boxer and the contrast between eighteen-month ministerial tenures and twenty- or thirty-year development cycles show why constant personal interventions destabilize procurement.

segments.title: Balancing innovation with program stability
segments.body: Long program cycles do not justify freezing technology while competitors continue to develop. Warhammer 40,000's fictional hostility to innovation provides an exaggerated picture of the stagnation that follows when inherited systems become untouchable. The opposite failure is changing direction every few minutes and never allowing a design or institution to mature. French practice offers a partial stabilizer because major procurement decisions can be embedded in legislation. A successor who wants a dramatic reversal must then introduce new legislation and explain the change publicly. The model is imperfect, but it creates a higher and more transparent threshold for disrupting a long-term force plan.

evidence.note: The transcript uses Warhammer 40,000 to illustrate the danger of treating innovation as forbidden while other powers keep developing.
French legislation as a way to require an explicit legal decision before a successor dramatically changes a procurement program.

segments.summary: Procurement must avoid both technological stagnation and constant reversal, with French legislation offered as one way to make major changes deliberate and visible.

segments.title: Why failures found in testing are good news
segments.body: Defence reporting often pushes every new system toward one of two extremes. Positive publicity presents equipment as unprecedented and dominant, while negative coverage calls it a useless rust bucket. Most aircraft, ships, and weapons fall somewhere between those caricatures. Reports of trouble during trials can be encouraging because testing is intended to find the faults that engineers and crews still have time to correct. The dangerous defects are those that remain hidden until personnel depend on the system in a war zone. Rigorous trials take equipment to its limits because combat will do the same, so visible development problems should be judged by whether they are identified and fixed rather than by whether they generate dramatic headlines.

evidence.note: Publicity may call equipment world-beating or useless, while actual performance usually lies between those extremes.
Aircraft and ship testing exposing problems that can be fixed before war, with rigorous trials deliberately pushing systems to their limits.

segments.summary: Defence coverage often labels new equipment either revolutionary or worthless, but faults discovered during demanding trials show that testing is exposing risks before war.
